title: History of Myanmar
wiki_lead:
The history of Myanmar (Burmese: မြန်မာ့သမိုင်း Myănma thămāing) covers the period from the time of first-known human settlements 13,000 years ago to the present day. Native to three imperial dynasties of South-east asia, the history of Myanmar is intertwined with the socio-political and cultural developments in the region over the past millennium. The earliest inhabitants of recorded history were Tibeto-Burman-speaking people who established an array of Pyu city-states that ranged as far south as Pyay and adopted Theravada Buddhism.
Another group, the Bamar people, entered the upper Irrawaddy valley in the early 9th century. They went on to establish the Pagan Kingdom (1044–1297), the first-ever unification of the Irrawaddy valley and its periphery. The Burmese language and culture slowly came to replace Pyu norms during this period. After the First Mongol invasion of Burma in 1287, several small kingdoms, of which the Kingdom of Ava, the Hanthawaddy kingdom, the Kingdom of Mrauk U and the Shan States were principal powers, came to dominate the landscape, replete with ever-shifting alliances and constant wars. From this time, the history of this region has been characterised by geopolitical struggles between the Bamar ethnic group, and the multitude of smaller ethnic groups surrounding them.
In the second half of the 16th century, the Toungoo dynasty (1510–1752) reunified the country, and founded the largest empire in the history of Southeast Asia for a brief period. Later Toungoo kings instituted several key administrative and economic reforms that gave rise to a smaller, more peaceful and prosperous kingdom in the 17th and early 18th centuries. In the second half of the 18th century, the Konbaung dynasty (1752–1885) restored the kingdom, and continued the Toungoo reforms that increased central rule in peripheral regions and produced one of the most literate states in Asia. The dynasty also went to war with all its neighbors. The Anglo-Burmese wars (1824–85) eventually led to British colonial rule.
British rule brought several enduring social, economic, cultural and administrative changes that completely transformed the once-agrarian society. British rule highlighted out-group differences among the country's myriad ethnic groups. Since independence in 1948, the country has been in one of the longest running civil wars involving insurgent groups representing political and ethnic minority groups and successive central governments. The country was under military rule under various guises from 1962 to 2010 and again from 2021–present, and in the seemingly cyclical process has become one of the least developed nations in the world.

Early history (to the 9th century)


Prehistory

The earliest archaeological evidence suggests that cultures existed in Burma as early as 11,000 BCE. Most indications of early settlement have been found in the central dry zone, where scattered sites appear in close proximity to the Irrawaddy River. The Anyathian, Burma's Stone Age, existed at a time thought to parallel the Lower Paleolithic and Middle Paleolithic in Europe. The Neolithic or New Stone Age, when plants and animals were first domesticated and polished stone tools appeared, is evidenced in Burma by three caves located near Taunggyi at the edge of the Shan plateau that are dated from 10000 to 6000 BC.
About 1500 BCE, people in the region were turning copper into bronze, growing rice, and domesticating chickens and pigs; they were among the first people in the world to do so. By 500 BCE, iron-working settlements emerged in an area south of present-day Mandalay. Bronze-decorated coffins and burial sites filled with earthenware remains have been excavated. Archaeological evidence at Samon Valley south of Mandalay suggests rice growing settlements that traded with China between 500 BC and 200 CE. grok_lead: The history of Myanmar spans from prehistoric human settlements in the Neolithic period through the development of early urban civilizations to the establishment of unified kingdoms, colonial rule, and modern political instability in the territory now comprising the Republic of the Union of Myanmar. Evidence of early habitation dates to Neolithic times, with the Pyu city-states emerging around the 2nd century BCE as the first organized polities, known for introducing Theravada Buddhism and sophisticated urban planning in central Myanmar. Positioned along ancient land and sea trade routes with India, the Pyu and Mon civilizations adopted Theravada Buddhism early and integrated Sanskrit and Pali terminology, Indian artistic styles, and legal frameworks, laying the foundation for the Buddhist architectural legacy seen in Pagan. The Pagan Kingdom (1044â1297 CE), the first to unify much of modern Myanmar under Burman rule, constructed over 10,000 Buddhist temples and monasteries, fostering a golden age of art, architecture, and irrigation-based agriculture before declining due to Mongol invasions and internal strife. Successor dynasties, including the Taungoo (16th century) and Konbaung (18thâ19th centuries), expanded Myanmar's influence across Southeast Asia through military conquests and diplomacy, only to face piecemeal annexation by Britain following the three Anglo-Burmese Wars (1824â1826, 1852, 1885). British colonial administration integrated Myanmar as a province of India until 1937, exploiting resources like teak and rice while exacerbating ethnic divisions through divide-and-rule policies. Myanmar achieved independence on January 4, 1948, amid promises of federalism that failed to materialize, sparking civil wars with ethnic insurgencies and communist groups that persist to this day. Military dominance intensified with Ne Win's 1962 coup, imposing isolationist socialism that devastated the economy, followed by the 1988 crackdown on mass protests, the 2011 transition to quasi-civilian rule under the military-backed USDP, and the 2021 coup overturning Aung San Suu Kyi's NLD government, reigniting widespread resistance and fragmenting control amid ethnic armed organizations' advances. These eras highlight recurring themes of centralization efforts clashing with ethnic diversity, resource-driven conflicts, and authoritarian resilience rooted in the military's self-perceived role as national guardian.
